overview: This is the yearly bill that authorizes funding and sets policy for U.S. intelligence agencies, such as the CIA, the National Security Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), for the 2026 budget year; the actual dollar amounts are in a classified annex. A major part reorganizes ODNI, the office that oversees all intelligence agencies, by eliminating or transferring several of its offices and centers, including closing the Foreign Malign Influence Center and moving some centers to other agencies. Other sections focus on China and Russia, artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies, security clearance reforms, and stronger protections for whistleblowers inside intelligence agencies. It also bars intelligence contractors from collecting or selling location data from phones at sensitive intelligence sites and extends a 2015 cybersecurity information-sharing law for ten years, to 2035. As of July 29, 2025, the Senate Intelligence Committee had filed its written report on the bill, which was on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say the bill trims overlapping offices to make intelligence agencies leaner, strengthens defenses against threats from China and Russia, and adds protections for whistleblowers and for personal location data.
against: Critics say closing offices such as the center focused on foreign influence could weaken the government's ability to detect foreign interference, and that much of the bill's spending stays hidden in a classified annex the public cannot review.
